sections.h: The end of the first Solomon collection and 'the words of the wise' (Proverbs 16–22)
sections.b: Proverbs 16:1–22:16 completes the first collection of 'the proverbs of Solomon'. Its two-line sayings use the second line to restate or extend the first more often than chapters 10–15 do, and they gather in small clusters: sayings about the LORD (Proverbs 16:1–9), about the king (Proverbs 16:10–15), about speech (Proverbs 18). Many reappear later in the book (Proverbs 16:25 and 14:12; 18:8 and 26:22; 20:16 and 27:13; 21:9 and 25:24). At Proverbs 22:17 a new section, 'the words of the wise', begins, with longer warnings addressed to a pupil and a close relation to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.

sections.b: "Wine is a mocker, and beer is a rowdy; anyone who reels under their power is not wise" (Proverbs 20:1). The saying casts drink as two of the book's bad characters, the mocker who scorns correction and the noisy brawler, and faults the person who is led astray by it. Proverbs 21:17 adds that the lover of wine and oil will not grow rich. The Talmud reads Psalm 104:15 in the same spirit: a moderate amount gladdens, too much makes a person crazy (Sanhedrin 70a). Churches have drawn different conclusions, from moderation to total abstinence.

sections.h: Proverbs and the Instruction of Amenemope
sections.b: Since Adolf Erman's study of 1924, scholars have seen that Proverbs 22:17–23:11 has close parallels with the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, a teaching in thirty chapters by an official to his son. Both open with a call to store the words in the 'belly' (Proverbs 22:17–18), aim to make the pupil a reliable messenger (Proverbs 22:21), forbid robbing the poor, befriending a hothead and moving boundary markers (Proverbs 22:22–28), and end with the skilled scribe who serves at court (Proverbs 22:29). Proverbs speaks of 'thirty sayings' (Proverbs 22:20) where Amenemope has 'Thirty Chapters'. The Hebrew sage adapts rather than translates, follows his own order, adds sayings of his own such as the warning on surety (Proverbs 22:26–27), and sets the whole under the LORD (Proverbs 22:19, 23).

sections.b: The LORD who weighs spirits and hearts (Proverbs 16:2; 21:2) recalls the Egyptian scene of the heart weighed on scales, and the 'cool' spirit of Proverbs 17:27 matches the Egyptian ideal of the silent man. On the close link between Proverbs 22:17–23:11 and the Instruction of Amenemope, see the ancient Near East page.

sections.h: Death and life in the tongue (Proverbs 16–18)
sections.b: "Death and life are in the tongue's hand, / and those who love it will eat its fruit" (Proverbs 18:21). Chapter 18 is the book's longest run of sayings on speech: the fool who only wants to air his opinions (Proverbs 18:2), gossip that slides down like treats (Proverbs 18:8), answering before listening (Proverbs 18:13), and the first speaker in a dispute who seems right until he is cross-examined (Proverbs 18:17). Around it, kind words are a honeycomb (Proverbs 16:24), a gossip splits up the closest of friends (Proverbs 16:28), and even a stubborn fool who keeps quiet is counted wise (Proverbs 17:27–28).

sections.b: "Train a young person according to his way; even after he grows old, he will not leave it" (Proverbs 22:6). The verb means to start or dedicate, and 'his way' may be the right way, the child's own aptitude, or his willful path; the saying states what usually happens, not a promise. Proverbs 22:15 assumes physical punishment: folly is bound up in a child, and the rod drives it out. Proverbs 19:18 sets a limit, read by Rashi as a warning against a blow that could kill. The Talmud set ages for the training of 22:6 (Kiddushin 30a). The Greek has no verse 22:6.

sections.b: "Showing kindness to a poor man is a loan made to the LORD, and he will pay him back for what he did" (Proverbs 19:17). Rabbi Yochanan said no one could say this if the Bible had not said it (Bava Batra 10a). Proverbs 22:9 blesses the generous eye, and Proverbs 21:13 warns that whoever shuts his ears to the poor will not be heard. In the Greek, Proverbs 16:6 reads 'by almsgiving and faith sins are purged', a form later cited in debates over almsgiving and forgiveness.

sections.b: These chapters see poverty clearly. The poor lose friends and even brothers (Proverbs 19:4, 7), have to beg (Proverbs 18:23), and fall into debt and slavery (Proverbs 22:7). Some poverty comes from laziness or love of pleasure (Proverbs 20:13; 21:17), but much from oppression (Proverbs 22:16, 22). Against this the sayings set firm values: a poor man with integrity is better than a liar or a fool (Proverbs 19:1, 22), rich and poor have one maker (Proverbs 22:2), and the LORD will argue the poor man's case in court (Proverbs 22:23).

sections.b: The longest run of royal sayings in Proverbs is 16:10–15, and more follow (Proverbs 19:12; 20:2, 8, 26, 28; 22:11, 29). The ideal king judges justly, hates wickedness, loves honest speech, keeps honest weights and holds his throne by loyal love and faithfulness. His anger is like a lion's roar and his favor like spring rain. Yet his heart is in the LORD's hand, who steers it like water in a ditch (Proverbs 21:1).

sections.h: Human plans and the LORD's purpose
sections.b: "A person's heart maps out his road, but the LORD fixes where his steps fall" (Proverbs 16:9). The sayings of Proverbs 16–22 return to this again and again: the answer of the tongue is the LORD's (Proverbs 16:1), the lot's verdict is his (Proverbs 16:33), his purpose holds (Proverbs 19:21), no one understands his own way (Proverbs 20:24), the king's heart is in his hand (Proverbs 21:1), and no wisdom stands against him (Proverbs 21:30–31). The sayings do not discourage planning; they set it under God (Proverbs 16:3).

sections.b: "People throw the lot into the lap, but every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). Proverbs 18:18 adds that the lot ends quarrels and separates powerful opponents. Lots were used to divide the land (Joshua 18:10), choose a culprit (1 Samuel 14:41–42) and, for the last time in the Bible, an apostle (Acts 1:26).

Proverbs warns repeatedly against guaranteeing another person's debt (Proverbs 17:18; 20:16; 22:26–27): the guarantor may lose his cloak or even the bed under him. "The one who borrows becomes the lender's slave" (Proverbs 22:7) describes real debt slavery, which the Law limited (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:1–18). The warnings on surety have no counterpart in the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, which Proverbs 22:17–29 otherwise follows closely.

sections.b: Proverbs speaks of wives both warmly and sharply. "The one who finds a wife has found something good, / and he draws favor from the LORD" (Proverbs 18:22), the same words Wisdom uses of whoever finds her (Proverbs 8:35), and a wife with good sense comes from the LORD (Proverbs 19:14). But a quarrelsome wife is a constant drip (Proverbs 19:13), and it is better to live on a corner of the roof or in the desert than with her (Proverbs 21:9, 19). The sayings are written for young men; the book balances them with its portrait of the woman of strength (Proverbs 31:10–31).
